newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu says Hebron deal within reach.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu says Hebron deal within reach.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday a U.S.-brokered deal on Israel's partial troop withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron was within reach.
But Netanyahu accused the PLO of stalling in some three weeks of negotiations, saying an agreement could have been reached days ago.
"I can say with certainty that with a willingness by the other side to conclude it, this thing has been possible for many days and it is also possible today," he told reporters.
Netanyahu spoke after meeting U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross who is trying to seal the elusive deal on security arrangements in the town of 100,000 Palestinians and 400 Jewish settlers.
Palestinians say the two sides are still far apart.
Ross, due to meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in Gaza later on Sunday, said a coming trip by Arafat to Europe would hamper mediation efforts.
"It's clear that we have further narrowed the differences that exist but we have not overcome those differences," Ross told reporters after meeting Netanyahu in northern Israel.

"Clearly the pace of negotiations is affected when the leaders are not here. Also my own presence is affected when the leaders aren't here because part of my mission is very clearly to go back and forth between the leaders," he said.
Arafat was due to leave Gaza on Monday on a European tour of several days.
Earlier on Sunday, top Netanyahu aide David Bar-Illan said the two sides were on the verge of an agreement which could be concluded at an summit between Netanyahu and Arafat.
Asked if Netanyahu would meet Arafat on Sunday, Bar-Illan said: "It may happen."
But Arafat's aide Nabil Abu Rdainah said no arrangements had been made for such a meeting.
"There are deep differences between the two positions. The same disputed issues are still disputed," said Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat.
He said the differences included Israel's demand for the right to pursue Palestinian militants into parts of Hebron vacated by Israel and what weapons Palestinian police would carry.

Israel's former Labour government agreed more than a year ago to redeploy troops away from Hebron but delayed the pullout after suicide bombings by Moslem militants killed 59 people in the Jewish state in February and March.
The right-wing Netanyahu, who ousted Labour in elections last May, has insisted on adjusting the agreement to help safeguard the Jewish settlers in the West Bank town.

In a sign of ever-present tensions in Hebron, a Jewish settler fired shots at Arab houses on Sunday but caused no casualties, Palestinian witnesses said. Israel Radio reported that two settlers had shot in the air after Palestinians stoned their car from rooftops.
Hebron settler Moshe Levinger told army officers at a meeting on Sunday that Jews in the town were concerned the agreement would lead to bloodshed.
"Levinger said they feel that this agreement gives them a feeling that they are under siege, that they are being choked," said army official Shlomo Dror, who participated in the meeting.
In a related development, Netanyahu put up for sale 3,000 homes built by the government in settlements across the West Bank, a government spokesman said.
Netanyahu lifted the previous government's restrictions on settlement activity in August but technical details had held up sale of the empty apartments.
"These issues have been cleared up and now apartments can be purchased by the public," the spokesman told Reuters.
The apartments were completed years ago but Israel's Labour government had blocked their sale.
